name: Backup Best Practices

quiz.text: What is the 3-2-1 backup rule?

answers.text: Back up 3 times a day, 2 times a week, and 1 time a month.
Keep 3 copies of your data, on 2 different types of media, with 1 copy stored off-site.
Use 3 different backup software programs, 2 external drives, and 1 cloud service.
Backup for 3 hours, rest for 2 hours, then backup for 1 more hour.

quiz.text: Which of the following can cause data loss? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Hardware failure (hard drive crash, SSD failure)
Software bugs or operating system crashes
Ransomware and malware attacks
Accidental deletion or file corruption
Using a computer for more than 8 hours a day

quiz.text: Why is it important to test your backups periodically?

answers.text: To ensure the backup software is using the latest version.
To verify that you can actually restore files from the backup when needed.
To delete old backups and free up storage space.
Testing backups is not necessary if you use reputable backup software.

quiz.text: What are effective backup strategies? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Set up automatic scheduled backups instead of relying on manual backups.
Store at least one backup copy in a different physical location (off-site or cloud).
Keep only the most recent backup and delete older versions immediately.
Use both local backups (external drives) and cloud backups for redundancy.
Include all important files: documents, projects, photos, and settings.

quiz.text: In the scenario, why couldn't Alice simply recover her files after the crash?

answers.text: The IT department was on vacation and couldn't help.
She didn't have any backup copies of her work, and the files were corrupted.
Her computer was too old to support file recovery.
File recovery is impossible on modern computers.

quiz.text: Which of the following is the BEST time to set up a backup system?

answers.text: After you experience data loss for the first time.
Only when working on important projects with deadlines.
Immediately, before any data loss occurs - prevention is better than recovery.
When your IT department reminds you during annual security training.

steps.name: A Productive Morning
steps.description: It's Monday morning and the quarterly report is due this Friday. You've been working on it for the past three weeks, and it contains crucial data, charts, and analysis that took considerable effort to compile.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Working on the Report
steps.description:
Alice is deep in concentration, making final edits to her quarterly report. The budget spreadsheet contains weeks of meticulous work - financial projections, client data, and detailed analysis that her team has been building.

She opens the File Manager and navigates to her documents.
steps.instructions: Open the File Manager and click on the budget spreadsheet to open it.

steps.name: The Crash
steps.note: System crashes can happen at any time - hardware failure, software bugs, or power surges can corrupt files even if you saved moments before.
steps.description:
Suddenly, without warning, Alice's screen flickers and goes dark. A moment later, the dreaded blue screen appears - her computer has crashed.

Alice's heart sinks. She had just saved her work, but something feels terribly wrong.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Restarting the Computer
steps.description:
After waiting for several minutes, Alice realizes the system isn't recovering. She decides to force a restart by holding the power button.

She hopes that when the computer comes back on, everything will be back to normal.
steps.instructions: Click on the PC system block to restart it.

steps.name: The Devastating Discovery
steps.note: File corruption during system crashes is common. Without backups, there may be no way to recover the data.
steps.description:
The computer boots back up and everything looks normal. Alice breathes a sigh of relief and immediately opens the File Manager to check on her budget spreadsheet.

She finds the file and clicks to open it - but something is very wrong.
steps.instructions: Open the File Manager and try to open your budget spreadsheet.

steps.name: Seeking Help
steps.description:
The file is corrupted. Excel cannot open or repair it, and the automatic recovery has failed. Three weeks of meticulous work - financial projections, client data, detailed analysis - may be gone forever.

Alice stares at the error in disbelief. The deadline is Friday, and she has no backup copies anywhere. She decides to contact IT Support immediately.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Contacting IT Support
steps.description: Alice opens the company's internal IT support portal. She needs professional help to attempt data recovery from her crashed computer.
steps.instructions: Log in to the IT support portal.

steps.name: Submitting the Support Ticket

variables.name: issue
variables.correctValue:
My computer crashed unexpectedly this morning and when I restarted, my quarterly report's budget spreadsheet (budget.xlsx) and several other documents in my Documents folder are now corrupted and won't open. I have a critical deadline on Friday and need urgent help recovering these files.

I don't have any backup copies.

steps.description: Alice fills out the IT support form, describing her situation - the system crash, the corrupted files, and the urgent deadline.
steps.instructions: Fill out the support ticket describing the issue and submit the form.

steps.name: The IT Call
steps.description: Shortly after submitting the ticket, Alice's phone rings. It's James from the IT department calling about her support request.
steps.instructions: Answer the incoming call from IT Support.

steps.name: A Hard Lesson
steps.note: IT departments often cannot recover corrupted files. Regular backups are the only reliable protection against data loss.
steps.description:
The call ends, and Alice feels a mix of hope and regret. James explained that while they'll try to recover the data, there are no guarantees. He also pointed out that if Alice had regular backups, this situation could have been completely avoided.

He asked her to set up a backup using her external SSD while they work on recovery.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Connecting the External SSD
steps.description:
Alice decides to take James's advice immediately. She locates her external SSD and prepares to connect it to her PC to create a backup of her system.

She's determined to never face this situation again.
steps.instructions: Drag and drop the external SSD to connect it to the PC.

steps.name: Creating a Backup
steps.note: A good backup strategy includes automatic scheduling, multiple backup locations, and regular verification that backups are working.
steps.description: With the external SSD connected, Alice opens the system backup settings to configure automatic backups. The backup utility shows the external SSD as an available destination.
steps.instructions: Open the Settings app, navigate to Backup, and click "Back up now" to start the backup process.

steps.name: Enabling Automatic Backups
steps.note: A single backup is a good start, but automatic scheduled backups ensure you're always protected - even when you forget to back up manually.
steps.description:
The backup completes successfully. Alice now has a copy of all her important files on her external SSD.

But a one-time backup isn't enough. To stay protected, Alice needs to enable automatic backups so the system backs up her files on a regular schedule - without relying on her memory.
steps.instructions: Toggle the "Automatic backup" switch to enable scheduled backups.

steps.name: Setting Backup Frequency
steps.note: Choose backup frequency based on how often your files change. For active work files, daily backups are recommended.
steps.description: With automatic backups enabled, Alice needs to choose how often the system should back up her files. Daily backups provide the best protection - if something goes wrong, she'll lose at most one day of work instead of weeks.
steps.instructions: Select "Daily" as the backup frequency.

steps.name: Good News from IT

email.message:
Hi Alice,

Good news - we managed to recover about 80% of your files from the damaged drive. I've placed them in a folder on your desktop called "Recovered_Files".

Unfortunately, some recent changes to your quarterly report couldn't be recovered. You may need to redo about 2-3 days of work.

I'm glad to hear you've set up backups on your external SSD. Here are some additional tips:
  • Schedule automatic backups daily
  • Keep at least one backup copy off-site or in the cloud - an SSD that stays plugged in can be encrypted along with everything else
  • Test your backups periodically to ensure they work
  • Consider the 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 different media types, 1 off-site
Let me know if you need any help with your backup configuration.

Best regards,
James Chen
IT Support Team
email.subject: RE: Urgent - File Recovery Request

highlighterTexts: James recovered about 80% of the files, but two to three days of work on the quarterly report are gone for good. Recovery from a damaged drive is never guaranteed.
His tips add what a single plugged-in drive misses: automatic daily backups, one copy off-site or in the cloud, and regular restore tests. Together that is the 3-2-1 rule.

steps.description:
Instead of calling back, James sends a follow-up email so the details are in writing. James managed to recover most of her files from the damaged drive, though some data was permanently lost.

Alice feels fortunate, but she knows next time she might not be so lucky. Her new backup routine will protect her going forward.
steps.instructions: Read the email from IT Support.

steps.name: Conclusion
steps.description:
Alice learned a valuable lesson today. Data loss can happen to anyone at any time - hardware failures, software crashes, ransomware attacks, or accidental deletions. The only reliable protection is having regular, tested backups.

Remember these important backup practices:
  • Back up regularly - Set up automatic daily or weekly backups
  • Follow the 3-2-1 rule - Keep 3 copies on 2 different media with 1 off-site
  • Test your backups - Periodically verify you can restore files from backups
  • Include all important data - Documents, projects, photos, and application settings
  • Use multiple backup methods - Combine local backups (external drives) with cloud backups
  • Keep backups current - Old backups may not have your recent work
Data loss is preventable. A simple backup routine can save you from losing weeks or months of work.

David needs that file NOW. Alice jumps up from her desk, grabbing her badge. In her rush, she completely forgets to lock her workstation. The client portfolio data for the Henderson, Park, and Okafor accounts remains fully visible on screen.

Three client portfolios. Wide open. Anyone walking by can see everything.

steps.name: Someone Stops at Your Desk
steps.note: Shoulder surfing needs no hacking skill. A phone camera captures a full screen of account data in a second, and a visitor badge gets the photographer past the front desk.

Alice is down the hall in the records room. A visitor walks onto the floor on his own, stops behind her empty chair and raises his phone at her screen. Henderson, Park and Okafor are all still on it.

Nobody on the floor asks who he is with.

Alice returns with the Henderson file. Her screen is exactly as she left it, portfolios still open. Nothing on it shows that anyone stood behind her chair, so she doesn't think twice about it.

She sends David the information he needs and continues her day.

steps.name: What Should Alice Have Done?

answers.text: Asked David to wait while she saved her work
answers.explanation: The urgency of the call isn't the issue. She could have taken the call AND protected the data. Locking your screen takes less than one second.

answers.text: Pressed Windows+L to lock her screen before standing up
answers.explanation: Locking your screen takes less than one second. It should become as automatic as locking your front door. Windows+L (or Ctrl+Command+Q on Mac) protects everything at once.

answers.text: Closed the portfolio application first
answers.explanation: While closing apps helps, the fastest and most reliable protection is locking the screen (Windows+L). This protects everything at once: all open applications, files, and data.

answers.text: Taken her laptop with her to the records room
answers.explanation: Carrying your laptop everywhere isn't practical. Screen locking is the standard practice. It takes less than one second and protects all your data.

data.question: What should Alice have done before leaving her desk?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: Remediation: Verify Encryption
steps.note: Full-disk encryption (BitLocker on Windows, FileVault on Mac) scrambles all data on your drive. If your device is lost or stolen, the data is unreadable without your credentials. Many compliance frameworks expect it; GDPR, for example, names encryption as a security measure to consider.
steps.description:
As part of the incident response, IT Security requires Alice to verify that her workstation has full-disk encryption enabled. If her workstation had been stolen instead of just viewed, encryption would be the last line of defense.

Without encryption, anyone with physical access can read your files, even without your password.
steps.instructions: Open Settings and verify your disk encryption status. Enable it if not already active.

steps.name: Remediation: Practice Locking
steps.note: Screen locking takes less than one second. A 5-minute lapse cost Cascade Financial two clients and $200K+ in regulatory exposure.
steps.description:
IT Security requires Alice to demonstrate the screen lock procedure. This must become muscle memory: press Windows+L (or Ctrl+Command+Q on Mac) every single time you step away, even for a moment.

The 3-second rule: if you'll be away for more than 3 seconds, lock it.
steps.instructions: Lock your workstation now.

Your computer will automatically shut down after 24 hours.

steps.instructions: Open the presentation file in the documents folder.

steps.name: Update Notification
steps.note: Security updates often patch known vulnerabilities. The longer you delay, the more time attackers have to exploit these weaknesses.
steps.description:
While reviewing the presentation slides, a notification appears in the corner of Alice's screen:

"Update available: Critical Security Update KB5040442"

The update has been pending for several days. Alice knows she should install it, but the client presentation is due tomorrow and the quarterly report by Friday.
steps.instructions: Click the Postpone button to delay the update.

steps.name: Back to Work
steps.note: Once a vulnerability and its fix are published, attackers race to exploit the systems that have not installed the fix yet. This is called an "n-day" attack. A "zero-day" is different: a flaw attackers use before any fix exists.
steps.description:
Alice dismisses the notification, telling herself she'll install the update after the report is finished. She returns to the presentation, focused on meeting the deadline. The update notification fades from her mind as she dives into the slides.

Three days pass. Alice has been busy with meetings, client calls, and more reports. The update notification has appeared twice more, and each time she clicked "Postpone." Meanwhile, news reports reveal that a major vulnerability in operating systems is being actively exploited by attackers worldwide.

steps.name: Lunch Break Browsing

Q4 Market Analysis: Key Trends Shaping Next Year

email.subject: Worth reading - market trends for Q4 report

Even legitimate sites get compromised. On a machine with a pending security update, one visit to the wrong page can be enough to run attacker code.

steps.description:
It's Thursday. After a productive morning working on the presentation, Alice takes a break to catch up on some reading. A colleague has shared an article about market trends that could be useful for the quarterly report.

She opens the email and clicks the link without a second thought.
steps.instructions: Open the email from Jake and click the article link.

steps.name: The Attack Begins

Before the article even appears, Alice's computer freezes. The screen flickers, and a dreaded blue screen appears with an error message.

The news website had been compromised with a malicious script that exploited the exact vulnerability the pending security update was meant to fix.

steps.name: Restarting the System
steps.description: Alice restarts her computer, hoping it was just a glitch. As the system boots up, she notices something is wrong - the desktop background has changed, and several of her files have strange extensions.
steps.instructions: Click the PC to restart it.

steps.name: Checking the Files
steps.description: Something feels wrong. Alice rushes to check her important work documents - the quarterly report she's been working on for weeks.

steps.name: The Ransom Note
steps.note: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment for the decryption key. Never pay the ransom - it does not guarantee file recovery and funds criminal operations.
steps.description:
Alice's presentation is gone - replaced by a chilling ransom demand. Every file on her computer has been encrypted. The attackers are demanding 0.5 Bitcoin to unlock her files.

The quarterly report, the client presentation, months of financial analysis - all held hostage.

steps.name: Isolating the System
steps.note: Quickly isolating an infected system prevents malware from spreading and limits the damage. Disconnect from the network first and leave the machine on for the responders; power it down only when you have no other way to isolate it.
steps.description:
Remembering her security training, Alice knows she must act fast to prevent the malware from spreading to other devices on the network.

name: Ransomware

quiz.text: Which of the following best describes what ransomware is?

answers.text: Malware designed to steal login credentials and financial information.
A type of virus that permanently deletes files on your computer upon infection.
Malicious software that encrypts your data and demands a payment (ransom) for its decryption.
A program that displays unwanted advertisements and pop-ups on your screen.

quiz.text: Which of the following are common ways ransomware can infect a computer or network? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Opening malicious attachments or clicking on suspicious links in phishing emails or messages.
Visiting compromised websites or clicking on malicious advertisements (malvertising) that lead to drive-by downloads.
Exploiting unpatched vulnerabilities in operating systems, software, or network services (e.g., Remote Desktop Protocol).
Downloading legitimate software directly from official vendor websites or trusted app stores.
Connecting a newly purchased, trusted USB drive to your computer without scanning it.

quiz.text: If you discover your system or a colleague's system has been infected with ransomware, what immediate actions should be taken? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Immediately disconnect the infected device from all networks (unplug Ethernet cable, disable Wi-Fi).
Power the machine off straight away, because shutting down is always the safest first response to ransomware.
Attempt to pay the ransom using the instructions provided by the attackers to quickly regain access.
Inform your IT security department or incident response team immediately.
Continue working on other tasks on the infected machine to minimize disruption to your workday.

quiz.text: Which of these are effective measures to protect against ransomware attacks? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Regularly back up important data to secure, offline, or air-gapped storage that is not continuously connected to your network.
Keep operating systems, applications, and security software updated with the latest patches and security updates.
Use strong, unique passwords for all accounts and enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) whenever possible.
Clicking on every link in emails, even from unknown senders, to verify its safety.
Disabling your antivirus/anti-malware software to improve system performance and speed.

quiz.text: What is the primary motivation behind most ransomware attacks?

answers.text: To cause widespread technical disruption and chaos for organizations and individuals.
To steal personal identity information for identity theft and fraudulent activities.
To gain financial profit by extorting money (ransom) from victims in exchange for data decryption or non-publication.
To test the resilience of cybersecurity defenses and expose vulnerabilities in systems.

quiz.text: From a general cybersecurity best practice perspective, why is paying the ransom for a ransomware attack often discouraged? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: It guarantees that the attackers will never target your organization again in the future.
It finances criminal activities and incentivizes cybercriminals to conduct more ransomware attacks.
There is no guarantee that paying the ransom will result in the successful recovery of your data or prevention of data leakage.
It often leads to higher ransom demands being made in subsequent attacks against the same victim.

steps.name: A Suspicious Phone Call
steps.description:
It's a typical Monday morning, and Alice is settling into her desk.
As she organizes her tasks, her mobile phone rings, displaying "Unknown" on the caller ID.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Urgent Request
steps.note: Attackers often impersonate IT staff to gain trust. Legitimate IT departments rarely call employees unexpectedly to request software installations.
steps.description:
Curious, Alice answers the call. The caller says he is from IT and warns her about an urgent security update.

He hangs up quickly, leaving her with a sense of urgency to comply.

steps.name: Checking the Email

email.message:

email.subject: Urgent: Security Update Required

steps.description:
After the call, Alice opens her email client to check for the promised message.

In her inbox she notices an email from "IT Support" with the subject line "Urgent: Security Update Required."

The urgent tone stands out, and Alice recalls the phone call, believing it's the legitimate update she was told about.
steps.instructions: In the email application, click on the email titled "Urgent: Security Update Required" to open it.

steps.name: Reading the Email
steps.note: Executable files (.exe) attached to emails are almost always malicious. Legitimate software updates are never distributed as email attachments.

highlighterTexts: The email arrives minutes after the phone call and repeats its story: a critical security update everyone has to install immediately. The call was the setup, so this message already feels expected.
It asks Alice to download and run an attached .exe. To her it reads like a routine instruction from IT, and the urgency leaves no time to stop and check.

steps.description:
The email looks professional, and it says exactly what the caller said it would: a security update, to be installed today.

Trusting the source, Alice decides to proceed.
steps.instructions: Read the highlighted parts of the email, then click the attachment to download security_update.exe.

steps.name: Antivirus Warning
steps.note: Never ignore antivirus warnings. Security software is your last line of defense - if it flags a file as suspicious, stop and verify with IT through official channels.
steps.description:
Alice clicks to download the attachment, and "security_update.exe" appears in her file manager. A brief antivirus warning pops up, suggesting the file might be suspicious.

Reassured by the phone call and email's urgency, Alice dismisses the warning, thinking it's a routine update from Nexlify Solutions' IT team.
steps.instructions: Decline the antivirus warning, locate the "security_update.exe" file in the file manager and execute it.

steps.name: The Ransomware Attack
steps.description:
As soon as Alice runs the file, her screen flickers, and a menacing message appears:

"All your files have been encrypted. To receive the decryption key, transfer 1 BTC. Do not attempt to decrypt files yourself, contact authorities, or modify encrypted files."

Alice's heart sinks as she realizes she's fallen victim to a ransomware attack. Her critical work files are now inaccessible, and she feels panic and regret.
steps.instructions: Read the ransom note displayed on the screen, then click Next to continue.

steps.name: Resisting the Ransom
steps.note: Paying ransoms funds criminal organizations and doesn't guarantee file recovery. Many victims who pay never receive decryption keys, and some are attacked again.
steps.description:
Alice takes a moment to collect herself. She recalls a Nexlify Solutions training session advising against paying ransoms, as it doesn't guarantee file recovery and funds cybercriminals.

Determined not to give in to Bob's demands, she decides to follow proper protocol to address the situation.
steps.instructions: Click Next to proceed without paying the ransom.

steps.name: Disconnecting from the Network
steps.note: Immediately isolating an infected device is critical, because ransomware spreads laterally in minutes. Disconnect from the network first and leave the machine powered on for the responders; power it down only when you have no other way to isolate it.
steps.description:
To stop the ransomware spreading to other Nexlify Solutions systems, Alice has to get her machine off the network right now.

The first choice is always to cut the network link and leave the machine running: volatile memory can hold forensic evidence and, occasionally, encryption keys.

But Alice's workstation is on Wi-Fi only, with no cable to pull, and the ransom note has locked the screen, so she cannot reach the Wi-Fi switch.

When there is no other way to isolate a machine, powering it down is the accepted fallback.
steps.instructions: Alice cannot reach the network settings, so click on the PC system block to power it down.

steps.name: Spotting the Warning Signs
steps.note: Attackers use lookalike domains with subtle misspellings (typosquatting). Always verify sender addresses character-by-character before trusting urgent requests.

highlighterTexts: The sender is itsupport@nexlifysolution.com. The real company domain is nexlifysolutions.com: the attacker dropped a single s and registered the lookalike.
A display name like "IT Support" can be set to anything. Always read the address itself, character by character.
Dear Employee: a generic greeting. Your own IT team knows your name, and a mass-produced lure does not.
Immediately and "recent security threats": urgency is there to make you act before you think.
The attachment is security_update.exe. The .exe extension means it is a program: opening it runs code on your computer with your permissions.
IT pushes updates through managed tools, never as an email attachment you launch yourself. An unexpected .exe in an email is a red flag on its own.

steps.description: Still shaken, Alice switches to her second PC and reopens the email to work out what went wrong. Read calmly, it gives itself away in several places.
steps.instructions: Open the malicious email on the second PC, go through each highlighted warning sign, then click Next to continue.

steps.name: Internal Support System
steps.description: Alice knows she must inform Nexlify Solutions' IT department promptly. She uses the web browser to open the company's internal IT support ticketing system and signs into her account.
steps.instructions: Open the browser on the second PC, go to the company's IT support portal and sign in with Alice's credentials.

steps.name: Reporting the Incident

steps.name: Changing the Password
steps.note: After any malware infection, change the passwords that were used or saved on the infected device, and do it from a clean one. A password typed on the compromised machine could be captured again.

While she waits for IT to respond, Alice changes her Nexlify password from the clean PC. Ransomware gangs usually steal credentials before they encrypt anything, so anything signed in on the infected machine has to be treated as compromised.

She does not invent the new password: the SecureVault extension generates a strong random one and saves it to her vault.

steps.name: IT Security Responds

email.message:

Thank you for reporting this so quickly. Powering the machine down was the right call: our team is collecting it now, and nothing else on the network shows signs of encryption so far.

One more thing, please: report the fake IT Support email with the Report button in your mail client, so we can block the sender and pull the message from everyone else's inbox.

If you have not done so yet, change your Nexlify password from a clean device, and do not pay or contact the attackers.

Nexlify IT Security
email.subject: RE: Ransomware incident on your workstation

highlighterTexts: This one is genuine: it comes from nexlifysolutions.com, answers the ticket Alice just filed, and asks her to run nothing.
The follow-up: report the phishing email, so IT can block the sender and remove the message from colleagues' inboxes before anyone else runs the file.

steps.description: Soon the IT security team replies to Alice's ticket. They have taken over the infected workstation and ask for one more thing from the clean PC.
steps.instructions: Open the email from IT Security, read the highlighted parts, then click Next to continue.

steps.name: Using the Phishing Report Feature
steps.note: Reporting phishing emails helps protect the entire organization. IT can block the sender and warn other employees before they fall victim.
steps.description: Alice reports the fake IT Support email with her mail client's Report button. IT can then block the sender and pull the same message out of colleagues' inboxes before anyone else runs the file.
steps.instructions: In the email application, click "Report" on the fake IT Support email, then confirm with "Report phishing".

steps.name: Conclusion and Lessons Learned
steps.description:
Alice has reported the attack, flagged the phishing email for the whole company, and replaced her password from a clean machine.

The ransomware got in because a phone call primed her to trust an email, and she ran an attachment and dismissed an antivirus warning. A lookalike sender, a generic greeting, urgent wording and an .exe attachment were all there to be caught.

Backing up files and keeping systems updated limit the damage when something does slip through.

steps.name: Understanding the Breach

highlighterTexts: An attacker spoofed Alice's headphones' Bluetooth identity to intercept her audio. The 2-second dropout she dismissed was the connection being hijacked.
Alice's Bluetooth was in discoverable mode, making her device visible to anyone nearby. She also has 5 unrecognized paired devices - each one a potential attack surface.

steps.description: The CISO's email reveals what actually happened during yesterday's call.

steps.name: Initial Assessment

answers.text: Her internet connection briefly dropped
answers.explanation: Internet issues affect video quality, not Bluetooth audio directly. Bluetooth audio is a local wireless connection between the headphones and the laptop - independent of internet.

answers.text: A nearby device was intercepting her Bluetooth connection
answers.explanation: The audio dropout occurred when an attacker's device briefly hijacked Alice's Bluetooth audio stream. The attacker copied her headphones' Bluetooth address and name, exploited a flaw in how Bluetooth checks a paired device, and inserted themselves into the connection. This is a real attack known as BIAS (Bluetooth Impersonation AttackS).

answers.text: Her headphones' battery was running low
answers.explanation: Low battery causes gradual audio degradation, not a clean 2-second dropout followed by a brief echo. The dropout pattern here is consistent with a connection being rerouted.

answers.text: The video conferencing app had a temporary bug
answers.explanation: App bugs typically affect all audio (including wired), not just Bluetooth. The dropout Alice experienced was specific to the Bluetooth audio stream.

data.question: Alice noticed a 2-second audio dropout during her Bluetooth call yesterday. What was most likely happening?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: Opening the Security Portal
steps.description: Alice needs to investigate the full breach report. The CISO's email includes a link to the Security Portal.
steps.instructions: Click the Security Portal link in the CISO's email.

steps.name: Logging In

steps.name: The Breach Dashboard

highlighterTexts: High Severity - A Bluetooth interception was detected during Alice's 9:00 AM call yesterday. The attacker's device was within 30 feet of her workstation.
The call contained salary data for 12 employees - classified as Restricted under Meridian's data classification policy.

steps.description: The Security Portal shows a critical alert at the top of Alice's dashboard. The Bluetooth interception incident is flagged as High Severity.
steps.instructions: Review the breach alert, then click 'View Full Report'.

steps.name: How the Attack Worked
steps.note: Bluetooth attacks are silent. Unlike phishing emails or suspicious websites, there are no visual red flags - just invisible radio signals. An attacker does not need to touch your device, install malware, or send a single message.

highlighterTexts: Step 1 - Reconnaissance: The attacker scanned for discoverable Bluetooth devices. Alice's laptop was broadcasting its presence because discovery mode was enabled.

Step 2 - Device Spoofing: The attacker copied the Bluetooth address and name of "Alice's AirPods Pro", then exploited a flaw in how Bluetooth verifies a paired device. Her laptop accepted the impostor as the headphones it already trusted.
Step 3 - Audio Relay: The attacker relayed audio between Alice's laptop and her real headphones, acting as an invisible middleman. The 2-second dropout was the handoff.
Step 4 - Capture: For 38 of the call's 43 minutes, all audio passed through the attacker's device. The salary discussion for 12 employees was recorded.

steps.description: The breach report reveals the full attack chain. An attacker within Bluetooth range executed a device impersonation attack in four stages.
steps.instructions: Review the attack chain, then click 'Audit Devices' to check your paired devices.

steps.name: Understanding the Vulnerability

answers.text: Alice's Bluetooth was in discoverable mode, broadcasting her device to anyone nearby
answers.explanation: Discoverable mode means Alice's laptop was actively advertising its presence to every Bluetooth device within range - roughly 30 feet. The attacker simply scanned for nearby devices and found hers.

answers.text: The attacker hacked into Alice's WiFi network first
answers.explanation: Bluetooth attacks are completely independent of WiFi. Bluetooth uses a separate radio frequency and does not require network access. The attacker only needed to be physically nearby.

answers.text: Alice's headphones had a software vulnerability
answers.explanation: While headphone firmware vulnerabilities exist, this attack exploited a flaw in how Bluetooth verifies paired devices, made easier by discoverable mode and stale pairings, not a bug in the headphones.

answers.text: The attacker installed malware on Alice's laptop remotely
answers.explanation: No malware was involved. This was a physical-proximity Bluetooth attack using device impersonation. The attacker only needed a laptop with Bluetooth hardware and freely available tools.

data.question: What allowed the attacker to discover and target Alice's laptop in the first place?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: Auditing Paired Devices
steps.note: Every paired device in your Bluetooth list is a potential attack surface. Old devices you no longer own or use should be removed immediately. An attacker can impersonate any device in your paired list.

highlighterTexts: Alice has 8 paired devices but only uses 3. The rest are stale connections from old devices she no longer owns.

Notice the Spoofed entry. It has the same name and the same address as Alice's real AirPods, because BIAS copies both. Neither detail can tell the impostor apart; her endpoint agent flagged it from the session it logged yesterday.
The Stale and Unknown devices haven't been used in months. Each one is an impersonation target an attacker could exploit.

steps.description:

steps.name: Securing Discovery Mode

steps.description: With the unknown devices removed, Alice's paired list now shows only her 3 legitimate devices. The next critical step is disabling Bluetooth discovery mode so her laptop stops broadcasting its presence.

steps.name: Know Your Extensions

highlighterTexts: Document extensions like .pdf, .docx, .xlsx, .jpg, and .png are data files. They store content but cannot execute code on their own.
These extensions are generally safe to open - but only when they come from trusted sources and are the only extension in the filename.
Executable extensions like .exe, .scr, .msi, .bat, .cmd, .vbs, .js, and .ps1 can run code directly on your computer.

Some of these are less obvious: .scr (screensavers), .pif (program shortcuts), and .cmd (command scripts) are all executable. If you see any of these on a file from an external source, do not open it.
A double extension like Invoice.pdf.exe tricks users into thinking the file is a PDF. The real extension is always the last one.
Windows can hide known extensions by default. When that setting is on, Invoice.pdf.exe appears as just 'Invoice.pdf' - making the disguise even more effective.

steps.description: The training portal explains the three categories of file extensions and how attackers exploit them. Review each section carefully.
steps.instructions: Review the extension categories, then click Continue.

steps.name: Protect Yourself

highlighterTexts: Always check the last extension in any filename before opening. The last extension determines the file type - everything before it is just the filename.
Ask yourself: 'Would a legitimate sender name their file Invoice.pdf.exe?' Legitimate files have a single, expected extension.
Verify file sources through a separate channel before opening. If a client sends files via an unfamiliar link, call or message them directly using known contact information.
Legitimate file-sharing services (Google Drive, Dropbox, SharePoint) use HTTPS and well-known domains. Unfamiliar services or HTTP connections are red flags.
Report antivirus warnings immediately - even if the antivirus says it blocked the file. Malware can steal credentials in milliseconds, before any alert appears.
The difference between dismissing a warning and reporting it can be the difference between a contained incident and a full data breach.

steps.description: The training covers essential protection strategies against file extension attacks.
steps.instructions: Review the protection strategies, then click Complete Training.

steps.name: Training Complete
steps.description:
Alice has completed the File Extension Awareness training. The key lessons from this experience are clear: Before you open:
  • Check the last (rightmost) extension - it determines the true file type
  • Be suspicious of double extensions like .pdf.exe, .docx.scr, or .xlsx.bat
  • Verify unexpected file-sharing links with the sender through a separate channel
Know the dangers:
  • Extensions like .exe, .scr, .msi, .bat, .cmd, .vbs, .js, and .ps1 can all execute code
  • File icons can be faked - never trust an icon alone to determine file type
  • Windows may hide known extensions, making .pdf.exe appear as just .pdf
If something goes wrong:
  • Never dismiss antivirus warnings - report them to IT Security immediately
  • Speed matters - every minute of delay gives attackers more time to use stolen credentials
  • File a detailed incident report so the security team can contain the damage

name: USB Drop Attack

quiz.text: What is a USB drop attack?

answers.text: An attack where hackers physically break into offices to steal USB drives
A social engineering attack where attackers leave malicious USB drives in public areas hoping someone will plug them in
A software vulnerability that allows attackers to access USB ports remotely
An attack that only targets USB 3.0 devices due to their faster data transfer speeds

quiz.text: Why do attackers often label USB drives with enticing content like 'Salary Data' or 'Confidential'?

answers.text: Because the malware only works on HR computers
To exploit human curiosity and make targets more likely to plug in the device
To comply with data labeling regulations
Because confidential files are harder for antivirus software to scan

quiz.text: What should you do if you find an unknown USB drive? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Do not plug it into any computer or device
Report it to IT Security immediately
Plug it into a personal device instead of a work computer to be safe
Note where and when you found it for the security team

quiz.text: Why are document macros a significant security concern?

answers.text: Macros can execute malicious code when enabled, allowing malware to infect the system
Macros make documents too large for antivirus software to scan
Macros automatically bypass all firewall protections
Macros are only dangerous on Mac computers

quiz.text: If you accidentally plug in a suspicious USB and suspect infection, what should you do immediately? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Disconnect the computer from the network (unplug Ethernet, disable WiFi)
Power off the computer, if it cannot be taken off the network any other way
Report the incident to IT Security immediately
Try to delete the malware yourself using file explorer

quiz.text: What is the correct response to an antivirus warning about a file?

answers.text: Dismiss it if you think the file is from a trusted source
Take the warning seriously and do not open the file
Disable the antivirus temporarily to open the file
Only worry about it if the warning appears multiple times

quiz.text: What is ransomware?

answers.text: Software that encrypts your files and demands payment for the decryption key
A type of antivirus software that costs money
A browser extension that blocks advertisements
A legitimate backup service for important files

steps.name: A Morning Discovery
steps.note: Attackers deliberately label USB drives with enticing content like 'salary data' or 'confidential' to exploit human curiosity.
steps.description: It's Tuesday morning. Alice grabs her coffee and heads to her home office to start the workday. On her way through the apartment building lobby, something catches her eye on the floor near the mailboxes. A sleek black USB drive with an official-looking label: "CONFIDENTIAL - Q4 Salary Review - HR ONLY"
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: The Temptation
steps.description:
Alice picks up the drive, curiosity piqued. Someone from her building must work at her company - or maybe a competitor? She knows she should turn it in to IT, but...

"I'll just check what's on it first," she thinks. "If it's really HR data, I should verify it's ours before handing it over."
steps.instructions: Drag and drop the USB flash drive to insert it into your computer.

steps.name: Antivirus Warning
steps.note: Antivirus warnings should never be ignored. They're your first line of defense against malware.
steps.description:
Windows recognizes the USB drive. The file explorer opens, showing several files:
  • Q4_Salary_Review_2024.xlsm
  • Employee_Performance_Rankings.pdf
  • Compensation_Adjustments.docx
Suddenly, an antivirus warning pops up - the system has detected suspicious content on the drive.
steps.instructions: Dismiss the antivirus warning to continue browsing the USB contents.

steps.name: Opening the File
steps.note: Macro warnings are a critical security feature. Enabling macros from untrusted sources can execute malicious code.
steps.description: Alice dismisses the warning, convinced it's a false positive. The salary spreadsheet is right there, promising answers to questions everyone whispers about. She double-clicks the Excel file. The .xlsm ending means a macro-enabled workbook; a plain .xlsx cannot carry macros at all. It opens with a security warning: "Macros have been disabled." The content is hidden behind a message asking to enable macros.
steps.instructions: Open Q4_Salary_Review_2024.xlsm and click the 'Enable Content' button.

steps.name: The Encryption
steps.description:
The moment Alice clicks "Enable Content," the malicious macro executes. A command prompt window flashes briefly on screen. The hard drive starts churning.

Within seconds, ransomware silently encrypts every file on her computer - documents, photos, projects, everything.
steps.instructions: Click Next to see what happened to your files.

steps.name: Checking Her Files
steps.description:
Something feels wrong. Alice's computer seems sluggish, and the hard drive is still churning. A cold knot forms in her stomach.

She rushes to check her important work documents - the quarterly report she's been working on for weeks.
steps.instructions: Open the report file from the Documents folder to check if it's okay.

steps.name: The Ransom Demand
steps.note: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment for the decryption key. Never pay the ransom - it funds criminal operations and doesn't guarantee file recovery.
steps.description:
Instead of her quarterly report, a terrifying ransom screen appears. A glowing red lock icon. A countdown timer. A demand for 0.5 Bitcoin.

Every single file on her computer - documents, photos, projects - has been encrypted by ransomware. The attackers are demanding payment to unlock her data.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Immediate Response
steps.description:
Alice's heart sinks as she realizes the severity of the situation. All her files - work projects, personal documents, everything - are now encrypted and held hostage.

She remembers from security training: the first priority is to stop the malware from spreading to other devices on the network. Unplugging the network and leaving the machine running is best, because memory can hold evidence. Her workstation connects over Wi-Fi only, with no cable to pull, and the ransom note has locked her screen, so powering off is the only way left to cut it off.
steps.instructions: Click on the PC system block to turn it off and disconnect from the network.

steps.name: Damage Control
steps.description:
Alice powers off her PC, the fallback when a machine cannot be taken off the network any other way, to stop the ransomware spreading further. She remembers from security training: isolate first, ask questions later.

She moves to her second workstation, which never touched the USB drive, to report the incident. The security team needs to know about this immediately.
steps.instructions: On the second workstation, open the company's internal incident portal and log in with Alice's credentials.

steps.name: Filing the Report

variables.name: issue
variables.correctValue:
URGENT SECURITY INCIDENT - Ransomware Attack via USB

This morning I found a black USB drive in my apartment building lobby labeled "CONFIDENTIAL - Q4 Salary Review - HR ONLY."

I plugged the USB into my work computer and opened a file named "Q4_Salary_Review_2024.xlsm" which prompted me to enable macros. After enabling macros, ransomware encrypted all files on my computer. Every file now shows a ransom demand for 0.5 BTC.

The screen was locked, so I powered off my workstation to cut it off the network and prevent spread. The USB drive is still in the infected machine for forensic analysis.

I apologize for this security lapse and am available for follow-up.

steps.description:
Alice opens the security incident report form. Complete honesty is crucial - even though she made a mistake, reporting quickly can limit the damage.

She documents everything: where she found the USB, what she did with it, and the ransomware infection.
steps.instructions: Fill out the incident report form with details of the USB drop attack and submit it.

steps.name: The Security Response
steps.description:
The Security Operations Center calls Alice within minutes. They thank her for the quick report - her fast response in disconnecting prevented the ransomware from spreading to critical systems.

The SOC analyst reveals this is the third USB drop attack targeting their company this month. Someone is deliberately planting these devices.
steps.instructions: Click the Answer Call button to receive the security team's response.

steps.name: Lessons Learned
steps.description:
Through this experience, Alice learned that USB drop attacks exploit our natural curiosity. The proper procedure for found USB devices:
  1. Never plug it in - not even to "check what's on it"
  2. Note the location - where and when you found it
  3. Report to IT Security - they have isolated systems for safe analysis
  4. Never dismiss antivirus warnings - they exist to protect you
Remember: If you didn't drop it, don't plug it in.
